title: Public-key encryption from one-way functions
formal: Does the existence of a classical cryptographic one-way function imply the existence of a classical public-key encryption scheme with negligible correctness error and security against uniform probabilistic polynomial-time chosen-plaintext adversaries? General constructions and security proofs may use the code of the one-way function; they need not be black-box.
definitions: A one-way function is a deterministic polynomial-time map \(f:\{0,1\}*\to \{0,1\}\)* such that every uniform classical PPT inverter I has negligible probability, for x uniform in \(\{0,1\}^{n}\), of outputting \(z\in \{0,1\}^{n}\) with \(f(z)=f(x)\) on input \((1^{n},f(x))\). A function \(\nu (n)\) is negligible if for every \(d>0\) it is eventually at most \(n^{- d}\). The scheme comprises uniform classical polynomial-time algorithms Gen, Enc, Dec. \(Gen(1^{n})\) randomly outputs public and secret bit strings \((pk,sk); Enc(1^{n},pk,b)\) randomly encrypts a bit \(b; Dec(1^{n},sk,c)\) deterministically outputs a bit or failure. For each b, the probability over honest generation and encryption that decryption is wrong is negligible. Security means that for every uniform classical PPT adversary A, in the experiment \((pk,sk)\leftarrow Gen(1^{n}), b\leftarrow \{0,1\}, c\leftarrow Enc(1^{n},pk,b)\), the advantage |\(\Pr [A(1^{n},pk,c)=b]- 1/2|\) is negligible. The adversary knows all algorithms and can encrypt arbitrary chosen bits itself with fresh randomness. This bit-message formulation extends to polynomially long messages by independent bit encryption and a hybrid argument. All runtime bounds are worst-case polynomial in the security parameter and appropriate input lengths. There is no shared secret before key generation, trusted setup, random oracle, quantum state, or auxiliary hardness assumption. Security is eventually negligible at all sufficiently large parameters, not merely infinitely often.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
why: This is the main unresolved boundary between the assumptions needed for private-key and public-key cryptography. It asks whether generic computational one-wayness already contains the structure needed to establish encrypted communication without a pre-shared secret.

importance.reason: A central minimal-assumption question in cryptographic foundations, separating the known reach of generic one-wayness from public-key communication.

progress.text: Impagliazzo and Rudich establish the fundamental oracle and black-box barriers to obtaining key agreement from one-way permutations; this also constrains public-key encryption constructions.
Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin, and Luby prove pseudorandom generators can be constructed from any OWF, establishing the generic route underlying private-key cryptography.
Barak and Mahmoody prove the quadratic-query attack on random-oracle key agreement. The result sharpens the oracle-model limitation without excluding arbitrary non-black-box constructions.
MIT’s foundations lecture explicitly presents PKE from OWFs as a major open question and distinguishes it from the established black-box separations.

Chatterjee, Mu, and Vasudevan construct PKE from planted MinRank hardness on random instances. The 2025 preprint appears at EUROCRYPT 2026; it adds a concrete foundation, not a reduction from an arbitrary OWF.

status_note: Explicitly open in the supplied MIT lecture. Research through 10 September 2026 found no standard-model implication from arbitrary OWFs alone or refutation of that general implication. The formulation fixes uniform classical adversaries and allows non-black-box constructions; oracle barriers and stronger concrete assumptions are kept separate.

context_blocks.text: A one-way function creates an asymmetry between evaluating a map and finding a preimage of a random image. Public-key encryption needs a different asymmetry: anyone holding the public information can produce ciphertexts, yet a receiver possessing related secret information can recover their messages. The question is whether this additional structure is implicit in every possible source of one-wayness.

One-way functions already suffice for pseudorandom generators and, through the standard chain of constructions, private-key encryption. There the honest parties initially share a secret. Public-key encryption removes that initial shared secret, so the existence of symmetric cryptography is not already a construction of the desired public-key primitive.

The classical obstacle is the Impagliazzo–Rudich black-box separation. Roughly, an idealized one-way-function oracle can supply private-key cryptographic hardness without enabling the necessary key agreement. A construction allowed to inspect and reason about a concrete function’s program lies outside the oracle interface, which is why the general implication remains open despite this barrier.

Public-key encryption would give a two-message key-agreement protocol: send a public key, then send an encryption of a freshly chosen shared secret. Barak and Mahmoody show a quadratic-query attack on key agreement built from a random oracle, matching the limited query advantage of Merkle puzzles. The theorem counts oracle queries and allows extensive other computation; it is not an unconditional attack on every standard-model encryption scheme.

New constructions continue to broaden the available assumptions. Chatterjee, Mu, and Vasudevan base public-key encryption on a planted MinRank problem over random instances, equivalently a rank-metric decoding assumption, rather than hiding a specially structured efficiently decodable code. This is progress in the choice of concrete hardness assumptions. It still assumes that specific problem is hard, a property not supplied merely by the existence of some arbitrary OWF.

sentences: A one-way function is easy to evaluate but hard to invert on a randomly generated input.
Public-key encryption needs a further asymmetry: anyone can encrypt using public information, while only the secret-key holder can decrypt.
This project asks whether the existence of one-way functions alone guarantees such an encryption scheme in the standard classical model.
Symmetric encryption follows from one-way functions, but its initially shared secret does not supply the missing public-key structure.
The question allows constructions that inspect the implementation of the underlying function, so limitations of black-box constructions do not settle it.
